notes: Finance figures are FULL-CYCLE candidate committee totals from OpenFEC /candidate/{id}/totals/ with full_election=true, i.e. the complete two-year cycle through 31 December of the election year. They are FINAL, unlike the 2026 figures elsewhere in this project, which are mid-cycle.

DISTRICT BOUNDARIES CHANGED INSIDE THIS WINDOW. 2018 and 2020 were run on the 2018 PA Supreme Court remap; 2022 and 2024 on the post-2020-census remap, which added Carbon County and changed the Monroe County portion. The seat is Lehigh Valley-based throughout, so the four elections are broadly comparable, but they are not the identical electorate.

Susan Wild's FEC candidate record is filed under district 15 for cycle 2018 (candidate_id H8PA15195-era numbering, H8PA15229), because she first filed in the pre-remap PA-15. A query of /elections/?district=07&cycle=2018 therefore OMITS her entirely. Her totals here were pulled directly by candidate_id.

In 2018 Wild simultaneously contested the FULL TERM in the new PA-07 and the UNEXPIRED TERM special election in the old PA-15 (both on 2018-11-06). Her single committee funded both, so her 2018 receipts are not a clean 'PA-07 general election' figure. The vote total used here is the FULL TERM (new PA-07) race.

Independent expenditures are OpenFEC /schedules/schedule_e/by_candidate/ aggregates with election_full=true, summed across committees by support/oppose indicator. These are deduplicated aggregates, not raw itemized Schedule E lines.

'Other votes' are third-party and scattered write-in votes reported in the official results. 2018 included a Libertarian (Tim Silfies) who took 3.0% of the vote; the other three cycles were effectively two-candidate races.

Two-party vote share (used for the correlation and regression) is a candidate's votes divided by the sum of the Democratic and Republican votes only. This is the standard comparable measure when third-party presence varies across years, as it does here.
extraction_problems: The FEC has published no compiled 2024 congressional election results file (only presidential). 2024 vote totals therefore come from the Clerk of the U.S. House's official Statistics of the Congressional Election, which is the authoritative source of record for House results, rather than from FEC.gov.

2018 finance is not strictly comparable to the other three cycles: Wild's committee financed two concurrent races (the PA-07 full term and the PA-15 unexpired term), and Nothstein likewise appeared on both ballots. No clean split of spending between the two contests exists in FEC data.

Candidate committee receipts understate total resources, sometimes severely. In 2024 Mackenzie's committee raised $1.8M against Wild's $9.0M, yet $9.4M of outside money was spent opposing Wild. Any finance-vs-results comparison that uses candidate receipts alone will mis-rank 2024.

The Clerk of the House summary for 2024 lists only the two major-party nominees and reports no all-candidate district total. Third-party and write-in votes for 2024 are therefore UNKNOWN and recorded as null, not zero — the 2018-2022 rows, which come from the FEC files, do report an all-candidate total. Two-party vote share, which is what the analysis uses, is unaffected.
n = 4 elections. This is far too small a sample for inferential statistics; regression output in this workbook is descriptive only and is labelled as such.
